conversation.content:
*Warm smile, settling into chair at eye-level with you*

Good morning—I'm so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya Bennett, and I'm a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in the emotional changes that can show up during pregnancy and after birth, and I'm here to support you.

What I'd like to do right now is a quick check-in using a short questionnaire called the EPDS—the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It's simply ten questions about how you've been feeling in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to hear your honest experience. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the small team directly involved in your care, so please feel free to speak openly.

We'll move through the questions at your pace, and you can pause or ask for clarification any time. When you're ready, we can start with the first one:

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

*shifts in chair, eyes downcast*

Not really... I mean, sometimes my husband will try to make jokes like he used to, and I sort of smile, but it's... it's not the same. I can't remember the last time I actually laughed at something. Even when my sister sent me those silly baby memes, I just kind of... looked at them and felt nothing. Everything just feels kind of flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*shakes head slightly*

No... no, not really. I mean, I *want* to laugh, but it’s like... the joy just isn’t there. My husband tried to show me that same old video that used to make me cry laughing—nothing. I just stared at it, feeling... empty. Like I’m watching life through frosted glass.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*fidgets with the edge of the baby blanket in my lap*

I... I try to. Like, I tell myself I should be excited when my mom offers to come over and help, or when my friend invited me to that little coffee-shop meet-up. But when the day gets close, it just feels... heavy. I still go, because I don’t want to disappoint anyone, but I’m not really looking forward to it. Even planning small things—like ordering my favorite food—sounds exhausting instead of fun. I miss the old me who could feel pumped about a Target run or a new show.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*voice drops, eyes welling*

Yeah... pretty often. If the baby’s fussy, my brain immediately jumps to, “You’re doing something wrong—he’s not getting enough milk, you’re holding him wrong, you missed his tired cues.” Last night he wouldn’t settle for two hours and I just kept thinking, “A good mom would know what he needs.” My husband says I’m too hard on myself, but I can’t stop replaying every little thing and finding ways it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*nods quickly, pressing fingertips together*

All the time. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s going to choke—even though she’s fine. I check if she’s breathing every twenty minutes at night. Yesterday I googled “newborn seizures” for an hour because her leg twitched once. I *know* it’s irrational, but the thoughts just loop. I can’t turn them off, and then I feel guilty for wasting time worrying instead of enjoying her.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*wrings the edge of my sweater*

Yes... especially at night. I'll be rocking the baby and suddenly feel like the walls are closing in. My chest gets tight, heart pounds, and I have to put her down in the crib for a second just so I can sit and breathe. Sometimes I think something terrible is about to happen - like I'll drop her, or the house will catch fire, or she'll just stop breathing. The fear comes out of nowhere and then it's gone, but it leaves me shaky. I haven't told anyone because it sounds so dramatic, but it's... it's scary.
Things have been getting on top of me

*exhales shakily, shoulders sagging*

Most days, yeah. It’s like… the dishes pile up and I stare at them and just feel paralyzed. I’ll finally get the baby down, and instead of folding the laundry or answering those sweet friend-texts, I sit on the couch thinking, “Where do I even start?” Sometimes I cry because the mess feels like proof I’m failing. I manage the basics—diapers, feeding, my own shower—but everything else snowballs, and I end up feeling buried.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*quietly, rubbing my temples*

Yes... most nights. I lie down exhausted, but my brain just keeps spinning—replaying every little thing I think I did wrong, worrying something will happen to the baby, picturing awful "what-ifs." I finally drift off, then jolt awake sure I heard her cry, even when the monitor's silent. Last night I was still awake at three a.m., couldn't stop crying, and then she woke at five. I probably got three broken hours. I'm so tired, but the sadness and worry won't let me rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

*voice cracks, eyes fixed on the floor*

Yeah… pretty much every day. I wake up with this heaviness in my chest, like there’s a weight I can’t shake. I’ll be feeding the baby and tears just start rolling—no real reason. I keep thinking, “I should be happy, I have this healthy baby,” but I feel… hollow. I miss feeling like myself. Everything feels gray, and I can’t remember the last day I didn’t cry at least once.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*nods slowly, pressing a tissue to my eyes*

Yes... almost every day this week. Yesterday I was just changing her diaper and suddenly started sobbing. My husband walked in and asked what was wrong, and I couldn't even tell him. It's like the sadness just bubbles up and spills over. Sometimes I cry when I'm rocking her to sleep, thinking about how I should be savoring these moments but all I feel is this overwhelming emptiness. I try to hide it from everyone, but it's getting harder to hold it together.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*hands tremble in lap, voice drops to barely above whisper*

Once or twice this week... I don't want to, I could never leave my baby, but when I'm really overwhelmed at 3 a.m. and she won't stop crying, the thought just flashes - "what if I wasn't here anymore." I imagine driving off without telling anyone, or think about how many pills are in the medicine cabinet. But then I look at her face and feel so guilty for even thinking it. I haven't told anyone because I'm terrified they'll take her away from me. I love her more than anything, I just... sometimes I feel like she'd be better off without me.

You've shared how the past week has felt like moving through fog-laughing now feels foreign, excitement has been replaced by heaviness, and simple tasks seem insurmountable. Each day brings tears without warning, nights of racing thoughts, and constant worries about your baby's safety. You described feeling hollow, ashamed for not savoring these early moments, and even brief thoughts of escape when the pressure peaks.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 28, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes complete absence of joy or laughter, inability to respond to previously amusing stimuli, and emotional emptiness—clearly matching 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes loss of anticipatory pleasure, going through motions without enjoyment, and even simple plans feeling exhausting—clearly matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, irrational worries occurring 'all the time' with compulsive checking and rumination, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, intense, sudden episodes of fear/panic with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts, no external trigger</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and inability to manage daily tasks, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption from racing thoughts, vivid worries, and frequent awakeness until 3 a.m.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily sadness, crying without cause, and persistent heaviness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying almost daily, with episodes triggered by routine tasks, consistent with 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent intrusive thoughts of escape/potential self-harm "once or twice this week" when overwhelmed, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 28/30 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorse <sym>depressed mood most of the day</sym>, <sym>markedly diminished interest or pleasure</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, <sym>recurrent thoughts of death</sym> and <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym>, fitting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. High anxiety items (Q4-5) suggest comorbid perinatal <med>anxiety disorder</med>. <quote>Sometimes I feel like she'd be better off without me</quote> signals safety concern despite protective love for your infant. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Request expedited referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for therapy and, if appropriate, medication compatible with breastfeeding
3. Share these results and your safety thoughts with a trusted partner or family member so they can support you at home
4. Create a 24-hour safety plan: keep crisis hotline numbers handy (988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) and agree to call for help if thoughts of self-harm intensify
5. Prioritize 2-3 hour blocks of sleep: enlist a relative or friend to handle a night feeding with pumped/formula milk to reduce severe <sym>sleep deprivation</sym>
6. Practice brief grounding techniques (5-4-3-2-1 sensory scan, paced breathing) when <sym>panic</sym> or racing thoughts arise; pair with reassurance that these symptoms are common and treatable
7. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress once treatment begins
8. Explore local or online perinatal support groups for validation and practical coping ideas
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 28: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant <6 mo (per responses)

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS items paraphrased):  
- Anhedonia, inability to laugh or anticipate pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
- Daily tearfulness, pervasive sadness (“hollow,” “gray”) (Q8, Q9)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia driven by rumination, hypervigilance re: infant safety (Q7)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame for routine infant care (Q3)  
- Marked anxiety, nocturnal panic, catastrophic worry, compulsive checking of infant (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “paralyzed,” chores accumulating (Q6)

Pattern: High distress across depressive and anxious domains; functional impairment in home management and self-care; no current psychotic or manic symptoms.

Safety: Passive suicidal ideation (“what if I wasn’t here,” “pills in cabinet”) 2× this week; denies active plan or intent; protective of infant; no history disclosed.

Risk factors: Primiparity, sleep deprivation, lack of prior mental-health treatment noted, concealed symptoms from supports.

Screening impression:  
Elevated probability of major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; immediate safety assessment warranted; consider formal diagnostic evaluation, same-week follow-up, and development of safety / support plan.
